I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a 19-year-old male with stalking trauma, body-focused shame is hard to reconcile unless there was physical or sexual assault. With the given trauma type, this item is clinically incongruent and stands out from the other appraisal items, which are otherwise plausible for stalking.

issues.item: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of stalking unless the stalker was also a trusted person. Because trauma type has already been fixed as stalking and no other node supplies context supporting an intimate or trusted-perpetrator stalking scenario, this item is clinically questionable in this profile.

issues.item: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' can fit only if the stalker was a trusted person, but the profile gives no other items in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Strategies to support an interpersonal-betrayal formulation. Paired with global characterological self-blame, this creates a specific relational-trauma narrative that is not otherwise represented in the self-report.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' is not impossible, but it implies the stalker was a trusted close other. The rest of the profile provides no supporting items in Memory, Threat, Triggers, or Strategies, and with no active formulation edges this appraisal stands as an unsupported trauma-specific claim. The other appraisal items ('I have to be on guard all the time', 'The world is a dangerous place') fit stalking more generically, but the betrayal item makes the node less coherent as a standalone set.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: These two items are not negative appraisals in the usual cognitive sense; they describe ongoing threat monitoring/safety behavior rather than evaluative beliefs. With a formulation showing no active edges and only the Negative Appraisals node populated, selecting predominantly hypervigilance/vigilance items makes the node content misaligned with the intended construct.

vignette: The first time Tariq realized he was being watched, it happened on a Tuesday evening outside the bus stop near his apartment. He had just stepped out of a late shift at the design studio, his canvas bag heavy with sketchbooks and a prototype tablet. A silver sedan had idled too long at the curb, its windows fogged despite the crisp air. He told himself it was nothing until the next week, when he found his studio locker slightly ajar, his personal charger missing, and a single folded note tucked inside that read, I know how you work. From that moment, the ordinary rhythm of his days fractured. He began replaying the weeks before it happened, searching for the exact moment his own behavior had invited the intrusion. He was certain the event happened because of the way he acted, convinced that if he had not posted his project milestones on his public portfolio or replied to that initial message from a stranger’s account, the whole thing would have stopped. The guilt settled in his chest like a stone; he blamed himself for the way he acted, parsing every past choice as a mistake that had left him exposed. By month two, Tariq’s apartment had become a series of mental checkpoints. He checked the deadbolt three times before bed, not out of habit, but because he had come to believe the world was a dangerous place where safety could vanish without warning. He told himself he had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, and that logic dictated every movement. When a delivery driver in a navy jacket walked past his window, Tariq’s breath would catch, his hand instinctively tightening around his coffee mug. The memory of the silver sedan still surfaced unbidden whenever a car idled nearby, his vision tunneling just enough to make him step back from the door. He stopped taking the route he used before, taking longer paths through well-lit corridors just to avoid the blind corners. Friends noticed the distance, but Tariq didn’t explain that his fear wasn’t about them—it was about the unpredictable way threats always seemed to arrive from places he thought were safe. His job as a UX designer, once a source of creative flow, became a landscape of quiet avoidance. He worked in an open-plan studio on the fourth floor, surrounded by glass walls and shared screens. During a late-week critique, when a colleague tapped him on the shoulder to show a wireframe, Tariq flinched so hard his keyboard clacked loudly across the desk. He had started leaving his phone on airplane mode during work hours, dismissing calls with quick texts. What frightened him most was the thought that his digital trail could still be visible, that every screen share or cloud upload might be leaving another door open. He began requesting video calls with clients instead of meeting in person, claiming it was for better screen clarity, though he knew the real reason was that he couldn’t risk being followed from a coffee shop to a co-working space. His design work grew quieter, his layouts more rigid, as if containing the interface might somehow contain the anxiety. Six months after the note, Tariq sat in a therapist’s waiting room, his hands folded tightly over his knees. He hadn’t slept through the night in weeks, waking instead to stare at the ceiling, counting the minutes until daylight. He had come to the clinic because the weight of constantly scanning the room, second-guessing every interaction, and carrying the certainty that his past choices had doomed him had finally outpaced his stamina. He wasn’t looking for a quick fix, just a way to stop feeling like the ground was constantly shifting beneath him. What he hoped for, more than anything, was to walk past a silver car without his pulse hammering, to trust that his own actions hadn’t predetermined his safety, and to finally design the kind of life where he didn’t have to watch his back to live it.
